name: Eigen
baseline: OpenBLAS 0.3.26 (also Intel oneMKL 2025.3 and AMD AOCL 5.2: AOCL-BLIS for BLAS, AOCL-libFLAME for LAPACK)
workload: Single-threaded nominal GFLOP/s of Eigen expressions (no external BLAS backend) against the reference BLAS/LAPACK routine on the same operands, for AXPY, DOT, GEMV, GEMM, TRSM, SYRK, POTRF, GETRF, GEQRF, SYEV, GESDD and GEEV in float and double, from 2x2 up to 16384-sized problems.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean of Eigen / library rate over square shapes, double precision (page's Summary table, above 1 means Eigen faster). GEMM vs OpenBLAS: 1.28 (n<=16), 0.95 (24-128), 1.30 (192-1024), 1.21 (1536-16384); GEMM vs AOCL-BLIS: 2.44, 0.88, 1.08, 1.24; GEMM vs oneMKL: 3.22, 2.19, 2.09, 2.00. TRSM vs OpenBLAS: 1.30, 3.55, 2.02, 1.24. POTRF vs OpenBLAS: 1.37, 1.26, 1.55, 1.20. GETRF vs OpenBLAS: 1.88, 1.56, 1.49, 1.07. SYEV vs OpenBLAS: 1.32, 2.21, 3.71, 2.56. DOT vs OpenBLAS: 4.89, 2.37, 1.18, 1.02, and AXPY vs OpenBLAS ~1.0 at large n. Single cells (double GEMM): 1024x1024x1024 142.7 GFLOP/s Eigen against 112.6 OpenBLAS (1.27x), 65.7 oneMKL (2.17x), 90.5 AOCL-BLIS (1.58x). Eigen is slower in places: GEEV at n 192-1024 (0.48 to 0.67), GEMV double at large sizes vs OpenBLAS (0.88), GEMM double 8x8 to 100x100 vs OpenBLAS (0.65 to 0.93), SYRK at n<=16.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma, C++17; Eigen master 15f227178 (5.0.1-dev), default configuration; Google Benchmark, 10 repetitions of at least 0.2 s per cell, median rate; one thread (OPENBLAS/MKL/BLIS/OMP thread counts set to 1), pinned with taskset
hardware: AMD RYZEN AI MAX+ 395 w/ Radeon 8060S (Zen 5, Strix Halo), L1d 48 KiB, L2 1 MiB per core, under WSL2 on Ubuntu 24.04.4 (Linux 6.18)
tradeoffs: Header-only template library, so BLAS-style calls are inlined into the caller (large part of the small-size wins is avoided call overhead into a shared library). Different API from BLAS/LAPACK: expression templates, aliasing rules (noalias), longer compile times, large template error messages. Eigen can also use an external BLAS/LAPACK backend through EIGEN_USE_BLAS, but these runs used none. Numerics follow its own algorithms for the LAPACK pairs (tridiagonal QR for SYEV, BDCSVD for GESDD).
caveats: First-party results by Eigen maintainers, published 2026-09-16 as the first dataset of a refreshed benchmark series; the comparison harness (benchmarks/comparison/ in Eigen merge request !2903, public) was still an open draft MR as of 2026-10-05 and the public pages are on libeigen.gitlab.io (blocked here, so the page source was read from the website repo's main branch). Run under WSL2 (absolute rates are a lower bound). OpenBLAS is the Ubuntu 0.3.26 package (DYNAMIC_ARCH, OpenMP build) running its Cooperlake kernel target on Zen 5, so it is not at its best on this CPU. oneMKL as shipped does not use its AVX-512 kernels on AMD CPUs (page's own caveat), which inflates Eigen's ratios against it; against OpenBLAS and AOCL-BLIS the gap is modest (about 1.0 to 1.3x for GEMM). Eigen was re-measured on 2026-09-16 at master 15f227178 while the library arms were measured on 2026-09-10/11 against an older Eigen master (4c3ac80d3); run-to-run noise is within 3% for 81% of cells and above 10% for 4%. Eigen's lead at n<=32 on AXPY/DOT is a ratio of fixed call costs (inline expression vs shared-library call), not kernel speed. Eigen is slower than the vendors on GEEV mid sizes and on several small GEMM sizes. Eigenvalue/SVD GFLOP/s use classical flop counts for both arms. Single machine, single thread, one CPU model; the older 2009-2011 Eigen benchmark pages (Core 2 Quad, MKL 10/11, GotoBLAS) are being retired by the project as unreproducible.

name: fbthrift
baseline: Protocol Buffers C++ (protobuf; version not stated), measured with SerializeToArray, SerializeAsString and SerializeToZeroCopyStream
workload: folly::Benchmark microbenchmark in thrift/lib/cpp2/protocol/benchmark: serialize and deserialize a struct of repeated field groups (i32, i64, 8-byte string, list<i32> of 10, map<string,i32> of 5, bool, double) in Small (1 group), Medium (3 groups) and Large (9 groups) sizes, Thrift Binary, Compact and cursor-based (CurSe) protocols against Protobuf equivalents (and an internal Carbon format).
claimed_speedup: Header comment 'Results for last run: 2025-11-18', time per iteration. Serialize Small: Thrift Binary 380.11 ns, Compact 395.36 ns, CurSe 230.85 ns versus Protobuf Array 945.69 ns, String 832.30 ns, ZeroCopy 998.08 ns (Binary about 2.2-2.6x faster, CurSe about 3.6-4.3x, derived from page data). Serialize Medium: Binary 936.16 ns, Compact 948.40 ns, CurSe 456.09 ns versus Protobuf 2.94 us / 2.55 us / 3.04 us (Binary about 2.7-3.2x). Serialize Large: Binary 2.72 us, Compact 2.75 us, CurSe 1.23 us versus Protobuf 9.54 us / 8.32 us / 9.60 us (Binary about 3.1-3.5x). Deserialize Small: Binary 396.13 ns, Compact 424.35 ns versus Protobuf about 660.7-681.1 ns (about 1.6-1.7x). Deserialize Medium: Binary 1.06 us, Compact 1.10 us versus Protobuf 2.08-2.18 us (about 1.9-2.1x). Deserialize Large: Binary 3.15 us, Compact 3.29 us versus Protobuf 6.58-6.68 us (about 2.0-2.1x).
compiler_and_flags: buck2 mode opt-clang-lto (Meta-internal fbcode build; clang version and protobuf version not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires the folly dependency stack and the Thrift compiler and IDL, which is a heavier build than protobuf; fbthrift diverged from Apache Thrift with its own cpp2 code generator, field_ref API, adapters and CursorBasedSerializer. Wire formats differ (Thrift Binary/Compact are larger or comparable but not identical to protobuf varint encoding).
caveats: First-party results pasted into a source comment (dated 2025-11-18); the benchmark code is public but CPU model, core count, clang and protobuf versions are not stated, and it needs the Meta fbcode/buck build, so it is not reproducible as published (tier C, not A). Serialize benchmarks time construction of the test object inside the loop for both Thrift and Protobuf (createThriftTestData / createProtobufTestData are called in every iteration), so the ratios mix object population with encoding; deserialize runs exclude the serialize step via BenchmarkSuspender. Protobuf rows copy into an IOBuf (SerializeToArray, SerializeAsString plus copyBuffer, ZeroCopy stream), a choice that may favour Thrift. One tiny synthetic schema, no strings of realistic length. fbthrift is described by the project list as Facebook's branch of Apache Thrift; is_fork_of left null because the upstream URL was not opened and cpp2 is largely independent code. Ratios are derived from the time/iter column; the file also lists a relative-percent column that agrees.

name: geogram (ParallelDelaunay3d)
baseline: CGAL 3D Delaunay triangulation (single-threaded; the paper also lists a CGAL Parallel column whose numbers were not captured)
workload: Runtime of 3D Delaunay triangulation / Voronoi input construction on synthetic clustered point sets (10 clusters) and density-gradient point sets, 100k to 15M points, in a third-party SIGGRAPH 2026 GPU Voronoi paper that uses Geogram and CGAL as CPU baselines.
claimed_speedup: Clustered points, Geogram versus single-threaded CGAL (seconds, from WebSearch result text of the paper): 100k points 0.060 vs 0.449 (about 7.5x faster, derived); 500k 0.250 vs 2.299 (about 9.2x); 1M 0.413 vs 4.808 (about 11.6x); 15M 5.890 vs 74.723 (about 12.7x). Geogram alone: 2M 0.792 s, 5M 2.024 s, 10M 4.072 s. Density-gradient set, Geogram 0.061, 0.282, 0.432, 0.882, 1.963, 3.804, 5.837 s for 0.1M to 15M points.
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars; Symposium on Geometry Processing Software Award 2023
tradeoffs: Geogram's ParallelDelaunay3d uses floating-point predicates with exact-arithmetic fallback (expansion_nt/PCK) and is multithreaded; it is a general geometry-processing toolkit with its own mesh data structures rather than CGAL's generic kernel framework. Input points may be perturbed or duplicated points handled differently from CGAL (not checked).
caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org and research.chalmers.se are blocked in this environment, so the paper (Taveira, Lindstrom, Fatemi et al., SIGGRAPH 2026, arXiv 2605.06408) was not opened; the numbers come from WebSearch result text that summarised its benchmark tables, and the two searches agreed with each other. Hardware, compiler, flags, thread counts, Geogram and CGAL versions are unknown. Geogram runs multithreaded while the quoted CGAL column is single-threaded (CGAL Parallel has its own column not captured), so the speedup mixes thread count with algorithm. The paper's own purpose is a GPU method, with Geogram and CGAL as baselines. Geogram's own README and wiki pages (Delaunay3D, Exact, BooleanOps) contain no numbers; a DelaunayBench repo that includes Geogram withholds its results. Tier capped at C because the source was not opened.
